I am the data protection officer of a hospital in the north of England, and I ask every supplier the same three questions. First: what exactly is recorded, and what is analyzed? Second: where is the footage stored, and for how long? In our hospital, footage is kept for thirty-one days, and then it is deleted automatically. Third: who can see it? Here, the footage can be seen by only three people from the security team, and every access is recorded. Suppliers with good answers to these three questions usually win the project. Suppliers who say, don't worry, it's all safe, usually don't.

Good afternoon. Let me explain how our system works, step by step. First, the video from each camera is sent to a small server in the hospital. One server can analyze up to sixty-four feeds. The images are analyzed in real time, and nothing is sent to the internet. When a person enters a restricted area, for example the pharmacy at night, the person is flagged on the screen, and an alert is sent to the security team. The alert includes a short video of ten seconds. In our last version, false alarms fell by half, because the system is trained with images from real hospitals.

I manage the nurses of a ward with forty beds, and most of our patients are older people. Falls are a big risk for them. Last year, cameras with fall detection were installed in every room. When a fall is detected, an alert is sent to the phones of the two nurses on duty. In the first month, we were not happy. There were too many false alarms, sometimes ten in one night. Then the system was adjusted by the supplier, room by room. Now almost all the alerts are real. And the most important thing: falls are seen in seconds, not in minutes.
